opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really useful lens. If you remember, AlphaGo was bootstrapped from human data. It started by imitating a large corpus of expert human games, and then reinforcement learning and self-play were layered on top to push it beyond that. AlphaZero dropped the human data entirely. It learned from scratch purely through self-play, with just the rules of the game, and it ended up stronger and discovering strategies humans had never really considered.

When I look at where we are with LLMs today, I'd say we're very much in the AlphaGo phase. We pretrain on this massive amount of human-generated text, we do supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, and then we apply RL on top, whether that's RLHF, or more recently RL with verifiable rewards on math and code, to sharpen the model's reasoning. The human prior is doing a huge amount of the heavy lifting, and RL is more of a refinement step that gets us a bit further along.

The interesting question is whether there's an AlphaZero moment ahead for language models, where RL becomes the primary driver of capability rather than a finishing layer. We're seeing early hints of that. Models trained with RL on reasoning tasks develop behaviors like backtracking, self-verification, and longer chains of thought that weren't explicitly taught. That suggests RL can elicit genuinely new strategies, not just polish existing ones.

But there are real obstacles to getting fully to the AlphaZero regime. Go has a perfect simulator and an unambiguous reward: you win or you lose. Most of the things we want LLMs to do don't have that. Math and code get close because you can verify answers or run tests, which is exactly why progress has been fastest there. For open-ended tasks like writing, research, or agentic work in messy real-world environments, defining good rewards and building environments is the bottleneck. So a lot of the frontier work now is really about environments and verifiers, because those play the role that the game rules played for AlphaZero.

So my view is that we're transitioning. We're still leaning heavily on human data, but the share of capability coming from RL is growing, and whoever figures out scalable environments and reward signals for broader domains is going to be the one who gets us closer to that AlphaZero-style leap.

r001.rationale: The response says current LLM training is in the AlphaGo phase: it relies on human-generated pretraining data and human demonstrations before RL refines the model.

r002.rationale: It asks whether an AlphaZero moment lies ahead, with RL driving capability, and describes emergent strategies not explicitly taught as early evidence of learning beyond human-provided examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think that comparison is actually a really useful lens for where we are right now.

So if you remember, AlphaGo was bootstrapped from human data. It started with supervised learning on millions of expert human games, and then reinforcement learning was layered on top of that to push it past what humans could do. That's very much where LLMs are today. We pretrain on this enormous corpus of human text, we do supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, and then RL, whether it's RLHF or the more recent RL with verifiable rewards on math and code, comes in at the end and sharpens the model. The RL is doing real work, but it's refining a prior that was almost entirely shaped by humans.

AlphaZero was the interesting next step, because it threw the human data away entirely. It learned purely from self-play against the rules of the game, and it ended up not just stronger but qualitatively different. It discovered strategies that human Go players had never considered, and it did that with far less human bias baked in.

I'd argue we are very clearly in the AlphaGo phase with language models, and we are nowhere near AlphaZero yet. And the reasons are instructive. In Go, you have a perfect simulator, a cheap and unambiguous reward signal, and a closed world. With LLMs, the "environment" is open-ended, the reward is often fuzzy or expensive to compute, and for most of the tasks we care about there's no equivalent of "did you win the game." Math and code are the exceptions, which is exactly why that's where we've seen the fastest RL progress. Those domains have verifiers, so they look a lot more like Go than, say, writing a good research summary does.

The other piece people underestimate is that the human prior is doing a lot of load-bearing work for us. In AlphaZero you could drop the human data because the game itself contains everything you need. For language, the pretraining corpus is the world model. I don't think you can self-play your way to that from scratch, at least not with anything resembling current compute. So the question isn't really "when do we get rid of human data," it's "how much of the capability can come from the model generating its own experience and getting feedback from the environment, versus being told by humans."

What I think the next couple of years look like is pushing more and more of the learning into that RL loop. Building better environments, better verifiers, longer horizons, agentic tasks where the model acts, observes consequences, and learns from that. That's the direction toward AlphaZero-style learning. But I'd be cautious about anyone claiming we're there. We've got a strong human prior and a thin layer of RL on top, and the exciting part is figuring out how thick that layer can get.

r001.rationale: It compares current LLMs to AlphaGo: pretraining and supervised fine-tuning shape a human-derived prior, with RL refining it afterward.

r002.rationale: It points toward more RL and model-generated experience, but does not clearly anticipate LLM learning becoming unbounded by human intuition; it emphasizes that the human prior remains load-bearing.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re closer to the AlphaGo stage than the AlphaZero stage. AlphaGo started by learning from human games and then used reinforcement learning to improve beyond that starting point. AlphaZero showed that, with the rules of the game and a clear reward signal, you could learn through self-play without first imitating human players.

With LLMs, we still rely heavily on that human foundation: pretraining on human-generated text, often followed by demonstrations, and then reinforcement learning. RL can improve the model’s reasoning, but it’s building on a substantial amount of knowledge learned from us.

The interesting question is what the AlphaZero equivalent looks like for language. In Go, you know whether you won or lost. For an LLM, what makes an answer good isn’t always so easy to verify. Math and coding are promising because you can often check the result. But for broader tasks, creating an environment where the model can explore and get reliable feedback is much harder. So I see the analogy as a direction to explore, rather than evidence that we’ve already reached that stage.

r001.rationale: It says LLM reinforcement learning builds on pretraining from human-generated text and often human demonstrations, paralleling AlphaGo’s human-game starting point.

r002.rationale: It describes an AlphaZero equivalent for language as a direction to explore and explains that AlphaZero learned through self-play without first imitating human players, anticipating learning less dependent on human intuition.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that AlphaGo started by learning from human games, and then used reinforcement learning to improve beyond that starting point. AlphaZero took that further: it learned through self-play, without needing those human examples.

With LLMs, we’re closer to the AlphaGo stage. We first train on a huge amount of human-generated text, often followed by demonstrations, and then use reinforcement learning to improve the model. So we’re still relying heavily on that human starting point.

The interesting question is what an AlphaZero-like approach would look like for language models. Could a model generate its own problems, attempt solutions, get reliable feedback, and keep improving? We’re seeing elements of that in areas like math and coding, where you can check an answer. But language is much broader than a game with fixed rules and a clear win condition. Creating that reliable learning signal across more open-ended tasks is a big part of the challenge.

r001.rationale: It says LLMs start from human-generated text and demonstrations, then use reinforcement learning to improve, and compares this to AlphaGo.

r002.rationale: It anticipates an AlphaZero-like approach in which a model generates its own problems, attempts solutions, and improves from feedback, moving beyond reliance on human examples.
